Let \(x_{(1)}\le \cdots \le x_{(5)}\). I use the usual Tukey/R boxplot quartiles for \(n=5\), i.e.  
\[
Q_1=x_{(2)},\qquad \text{median}=x_{(3)},\qquad Q_3=x_{(4)}.
\]

## (1) Boxplots, skewness, and ANOVA assumptions

Sorted samples:

- RU: \(31,56,78,143,210\)
- PS: \(26,30,37,54,70\)
- UC: \(21,22,24,36,65\)

Thus the five-number summaries are:

| School | Min | \(Q_1\) | Median | \(Q_3\) | Max | IQR |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| RU | 31 | 56 | 78 | 143 | 210 | 87 |
| PS | 26 | 30 | 37 | 54 | 70 | 24 |
| UC | 21 | 22 | 24 | 36 | 65 | 14 |

Text version of the boxplots:

\[
\begin{array}{rcl}
\text{RU} &:& 31 \;-\; [56 \mid 78 \mid 143]\;-\;210,\\
\text{PS} &:& 26 \;-\; [30 \mid 37 \mid 54]\;-\;70,\\
\text{UC} &:& 21 \;-\; [22 \mid 24 \mid 36]\;-\;65.
\end{array}
\]

The boxplots show that RU tends to have higher salaries: its median \(78\) is above every PS and UC observation. PS and UC overlap substantially.

However, RU also has much larger spread. The IQRs are \(87,24,14\), and the sample standard deviations are approximately

\[
s_{\text{RU}}=72.6,\qquad s_{\text{PS}}=18.3,\qquad s_{\text{UC}}=18.6.
\]

All three samples are right-skewed, especially RU and UC, with long upper tails/high observations.

The original ANOVA \(F\)-test p-value is \(0.06\). At the \(5\%\) level this is not formally significant, but it is borderline. The boxplots explain this: RU appears higher, but the very large within-RU variability and right-skewness inflate the error variance.

The usual one-way ANOVA assumptions are:

\[
Y_{ij}=\mu_i+\varepsilon_{ij},\qquad \varepsilon_{ij}\stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim}N(0,\sigma^2).
\]

The boxplots suggest violations of both approximate normality and equal variance. Independence cannot be checked from the boxplots, but assuming independent alumni samples, the main concern is the strong skewness and nonconstant spread.

---

## (2) Spread-versus-level plot and optimal power transformation

For each school, take

\[
\text{level}=\text{median},\qquad \text{spread}=Q_3-Q_1.
\]

Thus:

| School | Median \(m\) | IQR \(s\) | \(\log m\) | \(\log s\) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| RU | 78 | 87 | 4.357 | 4.466 |
| PS | 37 | 24 | 3.611 | 3.178 |
| UC | 24 | 14 | 3.178 | 2.639 |

Fit the spread-versus-level line

\[
\log(\text{spread}) = a+b\log(\text{level}).
\]

The least-squares slope is

\[
\hat b
=
\frac{\sum_i (\log m_i-\overline{\log m})(\log s_i-\overline{\log s})}
{\sum_i(\log m_i-\overline{\log m})^2}
\approx 1.57.
\]

For a power transformation \(Y^\lambda\), the variance-stabilizing rule from the spread-versus-level plot is

\[
\lambda = 1-\hat b.
\]

Therefore

\[
\hat\lambda \approx 1-1.57=-0.57.
\]

So the optimal power is approximately \(-0.57\), which on the usual ladder of powers is rounded to

\[
\boxed{\lambda=-\frac12}.
\]

Thus a reciprocal square-root transformation is suggested. In Box-Cox form,

\[
Y^{(-1/2)}
=
\frac{Y^{-1/2}-1}{-1/2}
=
2(1-Y^{-1/2}),
\]

which is monotone increasing in \(Y\). For the ANOVA \(F\)-statistic, using \(Y^{-1/2}\) or \(2(1-Y^{-1/2})\) gives the same \(F\), since they differ by a linear transformation.

---

## (3) ANOVA after transformation

Use

\[
Z=Y^{-1/2}.
\]

The transformed group means are approximately

\[
\bar Z_{\text{RU}}=0.1158,\qquad
\bar Z_{\text{PS}}=0.1597,\qquad
\bar Z_{\text{UC}}=0.1852.
\]

The ANOVA table for \(Z\) is:

| Source | df | SS | MS | \(F\) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| School | 2 | 0.012334 | 0.006167 | 4.116 |
| Error | 12 | 0.017981 | 0.001498 | |
| Total | 14 | 0.030315 | | |

Thus

\[
F=\frac{0.006167}{0.001498}\approx 4.12.
\]

With \(2\) and \(12\) degrees of freedom,

\[
p=P(F_{2,12}\ge 4.12)\approx 0.044.
\]

So after the reciprocal square-root transformation, the ANOVA gives

\[
\boxed{F\approx 4.12,\qquad p\approx 0.044.}
\]

At the \(5\%\) level, we would reject equality of the transformed mean salaries. The evidence for a school effect is stronger after stabilizing the spread, and the conclusion is mainly driven by RU being higher than PS and UC on the original salary scale.

{\sum_i(\log m_i-\overline{\log m})^2}
\approx 1.57.
\]

For a power transformation \(Y^\lambda\), the variance-stabilizing rule from the spread-versus-level plot is

\[
\lambda = 1-\hat b.
\]

Therefore

\[
\hat\lambda \approx 1-1.57=-0.57.
\]

So the optimal power is approximately \(-0.57\), which on the usual ladder of powers is rounded to

\[
\boxed{\lambda=-\frac12}.
\]

Thus a reciprocal square-root transformation is suggested. In Box-Cox form,

\[
Y^{(-1/2)}
=
\frac{Y^{-1/2}-1}{-1/2}
=
2(1-Y^{-1/2}),
\]

which is monotone increasing in \(Y\). For the ANOVA \(F\)-statistic, using \(Y^{-1/2}\) or \(2(1-Y^{-1/2})\) gives the same \(F\), since they differ by a linear transformation.

---

## (3) ANOVA after transformation

Use

\[
Z=Y^{-1/2}.
\]

The transformed group means are approximately

\[
\bar Z_{\text{RU}}=0.1158,\qquad
\bar Z_{\text{PS}}=0.1597,\qquad
\bar Z_{\text{UC}}=0.1852.
\]

The ANOVA table for \(Z\) is:

| Source | df | SS | MS | \(F\) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| School | 2 | 0.012334 | 0.006167 | 4.116 |
| Error | 12 | 0.017981 | 0.001498 | |
| Total | 14 | 0.030315 | | |

Thus

\[
F=\frac{0.006167}{0.001498}\approx 4.12.
\]

With \(2\) and \(12\) degrees of freedom,

\[
p=P(F_{2,12}\ge 4.12)\approx 0.044.
\]

So after the reciprocal square-root transformation, the ANOVA gives

\[
\boxed{F\approx 4.12,\qquad p\approx 0.044.}
\]

At the \(5\%\) level, we would reject equality of the transformed mean salaries. The evidence for a school effect is stronger after stabilizing the spread, and the conclusion is mainly driven by RU being higher than PS and UC on the original salary scale.
